If I had kept up my English, I would not be nervous before these calls.
If we had not lost that broker last year, we would be ahead of target now.
If I had not moved into the commercial side, I would not be running this region today.
If they had told us in March, we would not be redoing the plan this week.
Denise! Finally in the same room. How was the flight?
Long. I landed at six and the jet lag is winning. I flew this route in March and it took me three days to recover.
Three days. That is optimistic. And here we are, doing small talk in English, of all things.
I know. If we had met in Bogota, this would be a completely different conversation. But the room is half Italian, so English it is.
Honestly, my English gets better when I stop translating. Anyway — we never catch up properly. Two years of calls and always fifteen minutes.
That is my fault as much as yours. I am always swamped on Mondays. Before the others join — is there anything you want to land today that is not on the agenda?
One thing. The broker network. If Mexico had built what you built in the south, we would not be chasing the same three clients now. I want to steal your model.
Steal it, please. Let us circle back to that at lunch — I want to hear the whole thing properly, not in four minutes.
Lunch it is. And there is Milan, walking in nine minutes late, as always.
How was the flight? I did that route in March.
What are you working on that you actually enjoy?
Before the others join, is there anything you want to land today?
Let us circle back to that at lunch.
I would love to, but I am completely swamped until Thursday.

People get one thing wrong about small talk in a second language. They think they have to be charming. Funny, quick, with a good story ready. Nobody expects that. What people actually notice is whether you are interested, and that costs you almost no vocabulary. I have three questions I have used for thirty years. How was the journey. How long are you here for. And the best one: what are you working on at the moment that you actually enjoy? That last one gets you a real answer instead of a job title, and people remember who asked it. One more thing, about silence. When the language is not yours, two seconds of silence feels like twenty. It is not. To everyone else in the room it sounds completely normal. Let it happen. The person who is comfortable with a pause is the one who looks senior.

I run my week in three languages and I still get caught out. If I have spent the whole day in Spanish and then a call starts in English at four in the afternoon, the first ten minutes come out with the wrong shape. The words are English, but the sentences are not. For years I thought that meant I was losing the language. It does not mean that at all. It is simply the price of having three of them. What fixed it was two minutes. Before any call in English, I read something out loud in English, or I listen to two minutes of anything. Two minutes, and the machinery switches over. If I had not built that habit, I would still be spending the first ten minutes of every call apologising and warming up in front of the client, which is the worst possible place to warm up. Now the warming up happens before, on my own, and the client meets the version of me that already works.

How was the flight? I did that route in March and the jet lag took me three days. We never catch up properly. Two years of calls and always fifteen minutes. Before the others join, is there anything you want to land today? Let us circle back to that at lunch, when we have proper time.

If the group had approved the limits in March, we would be in a much better position now.
If I had not spent three years on the technical side, I would not understand these files at all.
If Milan had not been running late, none of that conversation would have happened.
If she had not moved across the room, she would still be waiting for an introduction.
